title: This historic Ontario town is known as Canada's most haunted
excerpt: Here's how to spend the ideal fall day in Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ontario.
content:
Ontario is home to many stunning spots, but one of its most beautiful towns is also one of its most haunted.

Tucked away about an hour and a half from Toronto in the province’s Wine Country sits Niagara-on-the-Lake, known to locals as “NOTL.”

Previously recognized as one of the 50 most beautiful small towns in the world by Condé Nast Traveler, visitors will notice Niagara-on-the-Lake’s well-preserved 19th century architecture upon arriving.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Niagara-on-the-Lake: A story of Canadian history

First shaped by Indigenous peoples before the War of 1812 “forged over the land,” the town became Ontario’s first designated National Historic District in 2003. It also gained a designation as a provincial Heritage Conservation District in 1986, according to Parks Canada.

“Every street in Niagara-on-the-Lake tells the story of Canadian history,” said Tourism Niagara-on-the-Lake.

But some of those stories are known to be haunted.

Niagara-on-the-Lake: Canada’s most haunted town

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Said to be “Canada’s most haunted town,” Niagara-on-the-Lake holds Ghost Walks every night in October until Halloween, along with select nights in November and December.

Expect stops at the legendary Prince of Wales Hotel and the Royal George Theatre.

Plus, visitors can also look forward to seeing the “infamous” Olde Angel Inn. With over 230 years of history, the Olde Angel Inn is home to more than just a place to stay in the area.

As the “popular local legend” goes, a Canadian militia officer named Captain Colin Swayze was killed at the inn during the American invasion of May 1813.

“Some believe the ghost of Captain Swayze is fated to walk the Inn at night, perhaps in longing for his sweetheart,” according to the inn.

To learn more about the inn, along with all of Niagara-on-the-Lake’s other haunted locations, tickets to the Ghost Walk can be purchased online for $17.

More to do in Niagara-on-the-Lake

Those looking for something a little less spooky can check out one of Niagara-on-the-Lake’s 40 wineries to experience “the birthplace of modern Canadian winemaking.”

For a stunning view while you sip, stop by Chateau des Charmes at 1025 York Rd. With tours and events, this spot is hailed as one of Ontario’s “most iconic” wineries.

Or take a stroll down Queen Street, which was previously named among the top 20 streets in Canada.

And only steps away is the Shaw Festival theatre, known as one of North America’s finest cultural attractions.

The Shaw Festival began in 1962 when lawyer and playwright Brian Doherty turned his love for the work of Irish playwright Bernard Shaw into a summer theatre festival.

Since then, it has grown into a Canadian cultural icon and gem. It hosts 10 or more productions each year in three Niagara-on-the-Lake theatres to audiences of more than 250,000 people.

For more history, Fort George National Historic Site is a major tourist attraction dedicated to the history of the War of 1812. During the war, Fort George was a military post that defended Upper Canada against American attacks. The site can be found at 51 Queen’s Parade.

After a long day of exploring, stop for a bite to eat at Bricks & Barley at 1573 Four Mile Creek Rd. or Niagara’s Finest Thai at 88 Picton St.
